name: Local-First Apps and Optimistic UI
intent: Let the screen read and write a database on the phone, so it reacts at once with or without a network, and send changes to the server in the background from a queue that survives the app being closed.
scenario: A to-do app handles 20 taps in a row. The network round trip is 400 ms, the server rejects 15% of requests, and the connection drops after the 14th tap. The app is closed 5 seconds after the last tap, still offline. We compare three designs: wait for the server, optimistic update with rollback, and local-first with a sync queue.
problem: An app that waits for the server before changing the screen is only as fast as the worst network the user is on. In a lift or on a train it shows a spinner, then an error. The common fix is an optimistic update: show the result first and undo it if the server says no. That makes the app feel quick, but the change still lives only in memory until the request succeeds, so a tap made offline vanishes when the app is closed, after the user was shown that it worked.

howItWorks.title: The screen reads local state only
howItWorks.text: The app keeps its data in a database on the phone (SQLite, or a store built on it). Every screen reads from that database and re-renders when it changes. The network is not on the path of a read or a tap, so the response takes the time of a local write, a few milliseconds, whatever the signal.

howItWorks.title: Writes go to the database first
howItWorks.text: A user action is applied to the local database in the same step as the screen update, and a record of what changed is added to a queue stored in the same database. Because the queue is on disk, it survives the app being closed, the phone restarting or the battery dying. Nothing the user saw succeed depends on memory.

howItWorks.title: A background sync drains the queue
howItWorks.text: A sync loop sends queued changes to the server in order whenever there is a connection. Each change carries an id, so a retry after a lost response is applied once and not twice. A failed request stays in the queue and is retried later with backoff. Pulling changes made elsewhere works the same way: fetch what is new, write it into the local database, and the screen updates by itself.

howItWorks.title: Optimistic updates as the lighter version
howItWorks.text: Without a local database you can still show the result before the server confirms: apply the change in memory, send the request, and if it fails, undo the change and tell the user. This needs a rollback path for every action and a message that explains it. It improves speed but not durability: a pending change that dies with the app is a change the user thought was saved.

howItWorks.title: Decide what a rejection means
howItWorks.text: Retrying fixes a failure of the network or of the server. It does not fix a change the server will never accept, such as an edit to something that was deleted or a value that fails validation. Those need a visible outcome: mark the item as not synced, say why, and let the user fix or discard it. Two devices editing the same data offline is a separate problem, covered in sync queues and conflict resolution.

pros: Taps and screens respond in milliseconds, on any network and fully offline
Nothing the user saw succeed is lost when the app is closed or the phone restarts
The app works the same in a tunnel as at a desk, so there is no separate offline mode to build and test
Sync is one background loop with retries, so the screens do not each handle network errors
cons: Two copies of the data exist, so you need sync, ids, and a plan for conflicts and for schema changes on the phone
The user can see something the server has not accepted yet, so the interface needs a way to show 'not synced' state
Validation and permissions still live on the server, so a change can be rejected long after the user moved on
A local database is more code, more storage use and more things to migrate than calling an API
whenToUse: Apps people use on the move, with weak or no signal: notes, tasks, field work, messaging
Interactions that must feel instant, such as ticking an item, liking, reordering or drafting
Data owned by one user, or edited by few people, where conflicts are rare and easy to explain
whenNotToUse: Actions whose result only the server can decide, such as taking a payment or booking the last seat: show a pending state and wait
Data that must never be stale, such as an account balance used to approve a transfer
Large shared datasets that cannot be copied to a phone, or that the user may not keep after access is revoked
pitfalls: Updating the screen optimistically with no rollback path, so a rejected change stays on screen
Keeping the pending changes in memory and calling the app local-first: they are gone when the process is killed
Queueing changes without an id, so a retry after a lost response is applied twice
Rolling back silently, so the user sees an item reappear and does not know why
Retrying a change the server will always reject, so the queue is stuck behind it forever
Never testing with the connection cut mid-request and the app killed, which is when the bugs appear

roles.label: User
roles.description: Taps, and expects the screen to respond at once.

roles.label: Screen
roles.description: Draws whatever the local database holds.

roles.label: Local database
roles.description: On the phone: the data plus the queue of changes not yet sent.

roles.label: Sync loop
roles.description: Sends queued changes when there is a connection and retries failures.

roles.label: Server
roles.description: The shared source of truth; it can accept or reject a change.

quiz.question: A to-do app updates the screen at once and sends the request in the background. The user ticks 6 items in a lift with no signal and closes the app. What is true about those 6 ticks?
options: They are kept, because the screen showed them as done.
They are lost, because the pending requests lived only in memory.
They are sent by the operating system when the signal returns.
They are rolled back with a message as soon as the app is closed.
quiz.explanation: An optimistic update changes what the user sees, not what is stored. With the request held in memory, closing the app discards it. A change persisted in an on-disk queue, as in a local-first app, would be sent at the next launch.

quiz.question: Which change makes an app respond in milliseconds even when the network round trip takes more than a second?
options: Compress the request bodies so each one is smaller.
Raise the request timeout so fewer requests fail.
Read and write a local database, and sync in the background.
Move the API to a server closer to the user.
quiz.explanation: The other options make the round trip cheaper or less likely to fail, but the screen still waits for it. Only taking the network off the path of a tap makes the response time independent of the network.

quiz.question: A local-first app queues changes and retries on failure. One queued edit refers to a list that another user deleted, so the server rejects it every time. What should the app do?
options: Keep retrying with backoff until it works.
Mark the item as not synced, tell the user why, and let them discard or fix it.
Delete the item silently so the queue can move on.
Retry the rejected change immediately in a loop, in case it was a glitch.
quiz.explanation: Retries help with transient failures, but a change the server will never accept blocks the queue forever. Dropping it silently loses the user's work without telling them. The user needs to see the outcome and decide.
